Once connected, open the intranet home page in your browser. 6. If it still fails, turn Wi-Fi off for ten seconds, turn it back on, and try the intranet again. Still stuck? Contact the IT help desk, tell them the VPN app says Connected but internal sites fail, and mention which Wi-Fi network you are using.

title: Authenticator app shows an empty account list
body: Symptoms: After you change phones or update the authenticator app, no accounts appear, or only some of them appear. You cannot generate codes for your work sign-ins. Cause: The accounts were stored on your old phone or in a backup that did not transfer to the new one, so this phone has no copy of them. Steps: 1. Confirm you are using the phone you originally set up for work sign-in. 2. Open the authenticator app, tap the menu, and look for Restore or Import. 3. If a cloud backup was turned on, sign in with the same account used for that backup and restore from it. 4. If no accounts come back, do not try to guess codes. 5. Contact the help desk. They will verify your identity and reset your authenticator setup. 6. Scan the new setup code shown on screen with the authenticator app, then type the current six-digit code to confirm. Still stuck? Call the help desk from a phone you can reach. Never share a setup code with anyone else, even a colleague.

title: Shared folder keeps asking for your password
body: Symptoms: When you open a shared folder from your file browser, a sign-in box appears again and again, even though you type the correct password. Files may open once and then ask for the password again later. Cause: Saved login details for the file share are out of date, usually from before a password change. Your computer keeps retrying the old password in the background. Steps: 1. Save any work and close all files opened from the shared folder. 2. Open the saved passwords area of your computer, usually found in Settings under Accounts. 3. Find any entry for the file share name and remove it. 4. Restart your laptop. 5. Open your file browser, type the share address, and enter your current password once. 6. Tick the option to remember the password only if your laptop is your own and locked when unattended. Still stuck? Contact the IT help desk and give them the exact name of the shared folder and the time the prompt started appearing.

title: Camera shows black or is not detected
body: Symptoms: During a video meeting, your picture is black, frozen on one image, or others say they cannot see you. The camera option may be missing from the video app settings. Cause: Another app, such as a photo editor or a second video call, may be using the camera, or the camera privacy setting on your laptop is turned off. Steps: 1) Close every other app that might use the camera, including web browser tabs with open calls. 2) Save your work and restart your laptop. 3) In the video app, open Settings, choose Video, and select the correct camera from the list. 4) Check for a physical privacy cover on your laptop camera and slide it open. 5) Open your system privacy settings, find Camera, and make sure the video app is allowed. 6) Rejoin the meeting and check the preview before you join. Still stuck? If you have an external webcam, plug it in and select it in the video app. Otherwise, contact the IT help desk with your laptop model and the name of the video app you used.

title: Others cannot hear you in a meeting
body: Symptoms: Participants say they cannot hear you, or your microphone level bar in the meeting does not move when you speak. You may see a muted icon next to your name. Cause: The microphone is muted in the meeting, or the wrong microphone is selected in the video app, or your laptop is sending sound to a different device. Steps: 1) Look at the meeting toolbar and click the microphone icon so it is not crossed out. 2) Open the video app Settings, choose Audio, and check that the microphone listed matches the one you are using. 3) Speak and watch the level bar; if it does not move, select another microphone from the list. 4) If you use a headset, make sure it is plugged in fully or paired over Bluetooth before you join. 5) Check that your laptop volume control is not set to zero and that the microphone is not disabled in system sound settings. 6) Ask a participant to confirm after you unmute. Still stuck? Leave the meeting, rejoin, and use the audio test option in Settings. If the level bar still does not move, contact the IT help desk.

title: Echo or feedback during calls
body: Symptoms: You or other people hear a delayed copy of their own voice, a high squealing sound, or a repeating echo during the meeting. Cause: Sound from your speakers is being picked up again by your microphone. This happens most often when two devices in the same room are in the same meeting, or when speakers are turned up loud. Steps: 1) Ask everyone in the same room to leave the meeting on all but one device. 2) Use a headset with a built-in microphone instead of laptop speakers. 3) Lower the speaker volume on your laptop to a comfortable low level. 4) In the video app Settings, open Audio and turn on the option to reduce background noise or echo, if it is available. 5) Move your laptop away from walls or other speakers in the room. 6) Mute your microphone when you are not speaking. Still stuck? Tell the meeting host that you are having echo problems and ask them to mute other participants who are in the same room. If the problem continues, contact the IT help desk and describe where the meeting took place.

title: Cannot join a meeting from the link
body: Symptoms: When you click a meeting link, nothing opens, you see a message saying the meeting has ended or cannot be found, or you are stuck on a waiting screen. Cause: The link may have expired, the meeting may have started at a different time, or the video app may not be installed or up to date on your laptop. Steps: 1) Check the time in the calendar invite against your clock, including the time zone. 2) Ask the meeting organizer to confirm the link is current and not from an older invite. 3) Copy the link and paste it into your web browser instead of clicking it in an email. 4) If the video app asks, allow it to open and sign in with your work account. 5) Update the video app from the app menu, then restart it. 6) Try joining by entering the meeting ID inside the video app. Still stuck? Ask the organizer to send a fresh invite and call the IT help desk with the meeting ID and the exact error message you saw.

title: Chat messages will not send
body: Symptoms: You type a message in the chat app, press send, and the message stays with a clock or error icon. Other people do not see it, or you see a message that says it could not be delivered. Cause: Your laptop has lost its internet connection, the chat app is signed out, or the chat app is still loading after a restart. Steps: 1) Check that your Wi-Fi icon shows a connection and that a web page loads in your browser. 2) Open the chat app and look at the top for a message saying you are offline. 3) Click the message with the error icon and choose the option to resend it. 4) If that does not work, sign out of the chat app and sign back in with your work account. 5) Restart the chat app completely by closing it from the taskbar or menu bar, then opening it again. 6) If you are on a work laptop away from the office, connect to the company VPN app before you try again. Still stuck? Copy the unsent message somewhere safe so you do not lose it, restart your laptop, and contact the IT help desk if the problem continues.

title: Chat notifications do not appear
body: Symptoms: You do not see pop-up alerts or sound when someone sends you a chat message or mentions you, even though the chat app is open. Cause: Notifications are turned off in the chat app, your laptop is in a focus or do not disturb mode, or the chat app does not have permission to show alerts. Steps: 1) Open the chat app and click your profile picture, then open Notifications. 2) Make sure desktop notifications and sound are turned on for messages and mentions. 3) Check that your status is not set to Do Not Disturb, which hides alerts. 4) On your laptop, open the system notification settings and confirm that the chat app is allowed to show notifications. 5) Turn off any focus or quiet mode you may have turned on for a meeting. 6) Restart the chat app and send a test message from another account. Still stuck? Check that your laptop volume is not muted, then contact the IT help desk with a note of which notification types are missing.

title: Video freezes or looks choppy
body: Symptoms: Your video or other people video stops moving, becomes blocky, or the voices fall out of sync. The meeting may say your connection is weak. Cause: The internet connection is slow or unstable, Wi-Fi is weak, or too many devices and apps are using bandwidth at the same time. Steps: 1) Turn off your camera in the meeting to save bandwidth and keep using audio. 2) Move closer to your Wi-Fi router or connect your laptop with a network cable if one is available. 3) Close large downloads, cloud file sync, and streaming videos on your laptop and on other devices in your home or office. 4) In the video app, open Settings and lower the video quality or turn off HD video. 5) Ask others on your network to pause heavy activities during the meeting. 6) Rejoin the meeting by connecting to your company network if you are working remotely. Still stuck? Restart your router if you have access to it, then contact the IT help desk with the time of the problem so they can check the network.

title: Meeting sound plays through the wrong speaker
body: Symptoms: You hear the meeting through your laptop speakers even though your headset is connected, or the sound cuts out when you move your headset or switch rooms. Cause: Your laptop is still using its built-in speakers, or the Bluetooth headset has disconnected or is paired to another device. Steps: 1) Click the speaker icon in your laptop taskbar or menu bar. 2) Choose your headset from the list of output devices. 3) In the video app, open Settings, choose Audio, and select the same headset under Speaker. 4) If your headset is Bluetooth, check its battery and make sure it is in pairing mode and connected. 5) Unpair and pair the headset again through your laptop Bluetooth settings if it keeps dropping. 6) Join a test call and check that you hear the test sound through the headset. Still stuck? Restart your laptop, then reconnect the headset before you join the meeting. If it still does not work, contact the IT help desk with the headset model.

title: Cannot sign in to the chat app
body: Symptoms: The chat app shows an error when you enter your password, keeps asking you to sign in again, or shows a blank screen after you sign in. Cause: Your password may have expired or changed, the sign-in session may be stuck, or the chat app may be out of date. Steps: 1) Make sure you are typing your work email address exactly as it appears in your staff directory. 2) Check whether your password was changed recently and try the new password. 3) Close the chat app completely and open it again. 4) If the sign-in page opens in your browser, clear the cookies for the site or try a private browsing window. 5) Update the chat app from its menu so you have the latest version. 6) Approve the sign-in on your authenticator app if you are asked for a second check. Still stuck? Wait ten minutes in case of a system delay, then contact the IT help desk and say whether the error message mentions your password or your account.

title: Screen sharing shows a blank or black window
body:
Symptoms: When you share your screen in a meeting, other people see a black box, a grey box, or only your desktop wallpaper instead of the app you chose to show.

Cause: The chat app can only share windows it is allowed to capture. If the setting is off, or the app you want to show is minimized or on another desktop, the share will look empty.

Steps:
1. Open the chat app and start or join the meeting.
2. Select the Share screen button and check the list of options.
3. Choose the specific window you want to show, not the whole desktop, if the desktop looks blank.
4. Make sure the window is open and not minimized before you select it.
5. If the share is still blank, quit the chat app completely and reopen it.
6. When prompted, allow the chat app to record your screen. On your laptop, go to the privacy settings for screen recording and turn the chat app on.
7. Restart your laptop if the option is already on but the share still fails.

Still stuck? Leave the meeting, then rejoin and try sharing again. If the problem continues, contact the IT help desk and tell them the name of the app you tried to share and whether it is a company or personal laptop.

title: Meeting keeps disconnecting
body: Symptoms: You join a meeting without trouble, but after a few minutes the call drops and you are returned to the start screen. Others may see you freeze or vanish, and you may need to rejoin again and again. Cause: The connection between your laptop and the meeting is unstable. This is often caused by a weak Wi-Fi signal, a laptop that switches networks, or a power-saving setting that pauses the network adapter. Steps: 1. Move closer to your Wi-Fi router or plug your laptop into a network cable. 2. Close large downloads, video streams and cloud backups running on your laptop. 3. Turn off Wi-Fi power saving: open Device Manager, find your network adapter, open its properties and untick the option that allows the computer to turn it off. 4. Restart your laptop, then rejoin the meeting using the link. 5. If you use a phone hotspot, switch to the office Wi-Fi or ask the meeting host to dial in by phone. Still stuck? Contact the IT help desk with the meeting time, your location and whether you were on Wi-Fi or a cable.

title: Screen share has no sound
body: Symptoms: When you share your screen, others hear nothing from videos or apps you play, though they can hear your voice. The silence can make your presentation confusing to follow. Cause: The meeting app sends sound only from the selected output unless the share-sound option is turned on, and some apps play sound through a different device. Steps: 1. Start screen sharing as usual. 2. In the sharing toolbar, look for a checkbox such as Include computer sound and tick it. 3. Choose the entire screen rather than a single window if the sound comes from another app. 4. Check your laptop volume is not muted and the correct speaker is selected. 5. Play a short clip to test, and ask a colleague to confirm they can hear it. 6. Stop and restart sharing if the option was missed. Still stuck? Tell the IT help desk which app plays the sound and whether your headset or laptop speakers are in use.

title: Camera image appears mirrored or upside down
body: Symptoms: Your video shows you reversed, so text on your shirt or badge looks backwards, or the picture is turned sideways. This can make you look different to colleagues and cause confusion during calls. Cause: Mirror or rotation settings in the chat app or camera driver are turned on, or the camera was installed at an angle. Steps: 1. Open the chat app settings and find the video section. 2. Look for an option named Mirror my video and untick it. 3. Check the camera preview to confirm the image is correct. 4. If the picture is upside down, open the camera settings in your laptop and choose rotate or reset. 5. Restart the chat app. 6. Rejoin the call so others get the corrected image. Still stuck? Contact IT and mention whether you use a laptop camera or an external webcam.

title: Stuck in the waiting room
body: Symptoms: You click the meeting link and see a message saying you are waiting for the host to let you in, but the host is already online and nothing happens. Others may think you have left the call. Cause: The meeting is set so that someone must admit each guest, and the host may not have noticed your request, or you joined from an unexpected account. Steps: 1. Wait one minute, then leave and rejoin with the same link. 2. Ask the host by chat or phone to check the waiting list. 3. Make sure you are signed in with your work account, not a personal one. 4. Close other windows showing the meeting to avoid duplicate sessions. 5. If the host cannot see you, ask them to add you to the meeting directly. Still stuck? Contact the IT help desk with the meeting title, start time and the host's name.

title: Recording button is greyed out
body: Symptoms: The record button in the meeting controls cannot be clicked, or it is missing for you altogether. You may need a recording for notes you are responsible for. Cause: Only hosts or people given permission can record, and some organisations turn recording off for certain meetings. Steps: 1. Check whether you are the host; hover over the controls to see the host label. 2. Ask the host to give you recording permission if you need it. 3. Open the meeting settings and check that recording is allowed. 4. If you are the host and it is still greyed out, sign out and sign back in. 5. Confirm there is enough free space on your laptop, since recordings need storage. Still stuck? Contact the IT help desk with the meeting link and say whether you are host or guest.

title: Live captions do not appear
body: Symptoms: You turn on captions but the box stays empty, or captions show only occasionally. Speech may appear in the wrong language. Cause: Captions need a supported language setting and a clear microphone signal; they can also be blocked by a policy or by a background noise filter. Steps: 1. Click the More menu in the meeting and choose Turn on captions. 2. Check the spoken language in the caption settings matches the language being used. 3. Make sure your microphone works by speaking and watching the level indicator. 4. Turn off any noise filter temporarily and test again. 5. Leave and rejoin the meeting if captions still do not start. Still stuck? Contact IT and say which language you speak and whether captions worked in other meetings.

title: Chat images will not upload
body: Symptoms: You attach a photo to a chat message, but it shows a spinning wheel or an error, and the message is never sent. The photo may look attached but never reaches the other person. Cause: The file may be too large, in an unsupported format, or blocked by a temporary connection issue. Poor signal can also interrupt an upload partway through. Steps: 1. Check the file size; most chat apps accept files up to a set limit. 2. Save the photo as a JPEG or PNG if it is in another format. 3. Reduce the image size using the photo app, then try again. 4. Check your internet connection by opening a web page. 5. Log out of the chat app and back in if the upload still fails. Still stuck? Contact the IT help desk with the file type, approximate size and the error text shown.

title: Virtual background will not load
body: Symptoms: You choose a background image, but your video shows your real room or the background is blank. Others may see a frozen or odd shape behind you. Cause: Your laptop may lack the graphics power for effects, or the background image file is not supported. Steps: 1. Open the video settings in the meeting app. 2. Choose a standard background image from the list instead of your own. 3. If you upload your own, use a JPG or PNG under a few megabytes. 4. Turn off other video effects like blur to save power. 5. Close heavy programs and restart the app. 6. If the option is missing, your laptop may not support it. Still stuck? Contact IT with your laptop model and the file type you tried.

title: Meeting invite is missing the join link
body: Symptoms: The calendar invite shows a meeting time but no clickable link or phone number. Others who received it may also be missing the link, so people arrive late or not at all. Cause: The organiser created the meeting without adding a link, or the invite was edited and the details were removed. Steps: 1. Open the invite and look for a join button or text with the meeting address. 2. Check the message body and any attachment for details. 3. Ask the organiser to resend the invite with the link included. 4. Open the chat app and look for the meeting in your calendar tab. 5. Do not guess a link from another meeting. 6. Keep the corrected invite in your calendar so you can find it later. Still stuck? Contact IT with the meeting title, date and the organiser name.

title: Unread messages will not clear in chat
body: Symptoms: The chat app shows a number badge for unread messages, even after you open every conversation. The number may not match the messages you see, which can be confusing. Cause: A message was marked unread by mistake, or a conversation is hidden in an archive or a closed channel. This usually happens after a network interruption. Steps: 1. Open each channel listed in the sidebar and scroll to the newest message. 2. Check the archived or hidden conversations section. 3. Right-click the channel and choose Mark all as read. 4. Restart the chat app and check again. 5. Sign out and back in if the badge persists. 6. Check your phone app too, as it may show a separate count. Still stuck? Contact the IT help desk with the number shown and the channel name.

title: Suspicious email asking for your password
body: Symptoms: You receive an email that claims to be from IT, HR or a well-known online service. It asks you to confirm your password, verify your account or fix a problem within 24 hours. The message may look official and include a company logo or a familiar signature. Cause: Attackers copy the look of real messages to trick people into typing their password on a fake page. The IT team will never ask for your password by email, and no legitimate service needs you to send it in a reply. Steps: 1) Do not click any links or open any attachments in the email. 2) Do not reply or send any details. 3) Report the message using the Report Phishing button in your email app. 4) Delete the email from your inbox and your deleted items folder. 5) If you already clicked a link or typed a password, change that password right away from a trusted device and tell the help desk. Still stuck? Contact the help desk by phone or chat from a different device, describe what the email said, and forward the email as an attachment to the security mailbox so the team can check it.

title: Fake login page that looks like the company portal
body: Symptoms: You open a link to the staff portal and the page looks almost right, but the web address is slightly different, the logo is blurry, or it asks you to log in again straight after you have already signed in. Cause: A fake copy of a login page was set up to capture usernames and passwords. These pages often arrive through links in emails, chat messages or search results. Steps: 1) Stop before typing anything into the page. 2) Look closely at the web address in the top bar and check that it matches the address you normally use. 3) If anything looks wrong, close the tab without entering details. 4) Do not use the link again. Instead, open the portal from your saved bookmark or type the address yourself. 5) If you already entered your password on the fake page, change it immediately from a trusted device and let the help desk know. 6) Report the link to the security mailbox, including where you found it. Still stuck? Call the help desk from a phone you trust, tell them what the page looked like and what address was shown, and ask them to check whether your account has been used from an unknown location.

title: Suspicious text message with a delivery or account link
body: Symptoms: You receive a text message on your work or personal phone saying a parcel is waiting, your account is locked, or a payment failed. It contains a short link and urges you to act quickly. Cause: Scammers send text messages in bulk hoping someone will tap the link and enter personal or work login details on a fake website. Steps: 1) Do not tap the link, even if the message seems to come from a delivery company or your bank. 2) Do not reply to the message or call a number listed in it. 3) If you are unsure whether the message is real, open the official app or website yourself and check there. 4) Report the text to the security mailbox, including the phone number it came from and a screenshot if possible. 5) Block the sender on your phone. 6) If you did tap the link and entered any details, change your work password right away and tell the help desk. Still stuck? Contact the help desk by phone and describe the message. Do not forward the link to colleagues, because they could tap it by accident.

title: Unexpected sign-in approval prompts on your phone
body: Symptoms: Your authenticator app keeps sending approval requests that you did not start, sometimes late at night or early in the morning. You may feel pressure to tap approve just to make the notifications stop. Cause: An attacker has your password and is trying to sign in. Each request needs your approval, and they hope you will tap approve by mistake or out of frustration. This trick is called approval fatigue. Steps: 1) Tap Deny on every request you did not start. 2) Do not approve a request just because you keep getting them. 3) Change your work password from a trusted device. 4) Open your authenticator app and check for any new devices you do not recognise, then remove them. 5) Report the activity to the security mailbox with the times you saw the prompts. 6) Watch your email for password reset messages you did not request. Still stuck? Call the help desk from a phone number on file, rather than replying to any notification. The team can review sign-in logs, reset your sign-in settings and confirm that your account is safe.

title: Lost or stolen laptop or phone
body: Symptoms: You cannot find your laptop or work phone after leaving it in a car, a café, a train or the office. You may remember last seeing it some time ago and wonder whether someone else has picked it up. Cause: Portable devices are easy to lose or steal, and they may hold saved emails, files and sign-in sessions that someone could misuse. Quick reporting limits the damage. Steps: 1) Report the loss to the help desk as soon as you notice, even if you are not sure it is gone. 2) Give your name, device type and the last place and time you had it. 3) From another device, sign in to the company account page and sign out of all sessions. 4) Change your work password from a trusted device. 5) If your phone is enrolled in mobile management, ask the help desk to send a remote lock or wipe. 6) Do not try to recover the device yourself, and do not confront anyone who may have it. 7) If it was stolen, report it to local police too and keep the reference number. Still stuck? Contact the help desk by phone and wait for confirmation that the device is locked before you return to your normal work.

title: You opened an attachment you now think was unsafe
body: Symptoms: You opened a file from an email, such as a document, spreadsheet or zip file, and now your laptop is running slowly, shows pop-up windows, or a message asks you to enable macros or content. You may feel worried that you made a mistake. Cause: Malicious attachments can install software that spies on activity or locks files. Many arrive pretending to be invoices, shipping notices or shared documents from people you know. Steps: 1) Disconnect your laptop from Wi-Fi and unplug any network cable. Do not switch it off yet, because the help desk may need to look at it. 2) Do not enter any passwords or click any further prompts. 3) Call the help desk straight away and tell them which file you opened and roughly when. 4) Do not open the same file on another computer. 5) Keep the original email, since it helps the security team find similar messages. 6) Follow any instructions the help desk gives you about changing passwords. Still stuck? Staff are trained to handle this situation calmly. Telling the team quickly, even if you only feel unsure, is always better than waiting to see whether anything happens.

title: Fake invoice or payment change request
body: Symptoms: You receive an email that appears to come from a supplier or a senior colleague asking you to pay an invoice to a new bank account, or urgently process a payment before the end of the day. The tone may be polite but pressing, and it may ask you to keep the request confidential. Cause: This is a common fraud called business email compromise. Attackers either copy a real supplier address or take over a real mailbox, then ask for payments to go to their own account. Steps: 1) Do not change any bank details or make the payment yet. 2) Check the request by calling the supplier or colleague on a phone number you already have on file, not one from the email. 3) Look closely at the sender address for small spelling changes. 4) Report the email to the security mailbox and to the finance team. 5) If you already sent a payment, tell finance and the help desk immediately, because quick action can sometimes stop the money. 6) Follow the company rule that any change to bank details needs a second approver. Still stuck? Contact finance and the help desk for advice. A short delay to check is always acceptable, even when the request says it is urgent.

title: Phone call from someone claiming to be IT support
body: Symptoms: A caller says they are from the IT team, mentions your name or department, and says they need you to read out a code, install a remote support tool or confirm your password to fix an urgent problem. They may sound busy, friendly or slightly impatient. Cause: Fraudsters use phone calls to build trust and get access quickly. Real IT staff will never ask for your password, one-time codes or permission to install software during an unexpected call. Steps: 1) Do not share any password, code or personal detail. 2) Do not install any software the caller asks for. 3) Politely say you will call back using the official help desk number. 4) Hang up and dial the number from the staff directory or the back of your ID badge. 5) Tell the help desk what happened, including the caller's name and the number they used. 6) If you already shared a code or password, change your password from a trusted device and tell the team at once. 7) Report the call to the security mailbox. Still stuck? Ask the help desk to check whether anyone has tried to sign in to your account recently, and follow their guidance on next steps.

title: You typed your work password into the wrong website
body: Symptoms: You realise after entering your work password that the page you were on was not the official site. It may have been a page you reached from a search result, a link in a chat or a pop-up while browsing. The page may have asked you to sign in again or shown an error message. Cause: Fake websites copy real login screens to collect passwords. Once a password is typed, it can be used by the person who set up the page, often within minutes. Steps: 1) Close the page without clicking anything else on it. 2) Change your work password right away from a device you trust, using the official portal address. 3) If you use the same password anywhere else, change it there too. 4) Check your account activity page for sign-ins you do not recognise. 5) Tell the help desk what you typed and roughly when, so they can review your account. 6) Report the website address to the security mailbox so it can be blocked for everyone. 7) In future, use a password manager where allowed, because it will not fill in your password on a page with a different address. Still stuck? Contact the help desk by phone and ask them to confirm that your account has been secured and that multi-factor sign-in is still active.

title: Found a USB stick or shared a password by mistake
body: Symptoms: You find an unlabelled USB stick in the office or car park, or a colleague asks you to share your password so they can access a file quickly. You may be unsure whether it is safe to plug in the stick or whether the request is reasonable. Cause: Lost USB sticks are a common way for malicious software to spread, because curious people plug them in to find the owner. Sharing passwords is also risky, because it means your account can be used by someone else and makes it hard to tell who did what. Steps: 1) Do not plug the USB stick into any company computer or personal device. 2) Hand it to the help desk or leave it at the reception desk with a note saying where you found it. 3) Never share your password, even with colleagues or managers. 4) If someone needs access to a file, ask the file owner to grant them permission through the shared folder system. 5) If you already shared your password, change it immediately and tell the help desk. 6) Remember that IT staff can add access without needing your password. Still stuck? Contact the help desk for advice on getting access to shared files, or to arrange safe disposal or review of any unknown device.

title: You shared a file link with the wrong person
body: Symptoms: You realise a shared document link was sent to someone outside the team, or to a person who should not see the file. You may see an access notification from an unknown address. Cause: Links to files can be forwarded, and sharing settings may be set to anyone with the link. Steps: 1. Stop sharing the file straight away by opening the file, selecting Share, and removing the wrong person or changing the link access to restricted. 2. Check the access list to see if anyone else was added. 3. Do not delete the file, as this can hide what was viewed. 4. Write down the date, time, file name, and the email address the link was sent to. 5. Send a short message to the IT help desk with those details so they can check the access log. Still stuck? If you cannot change the sharing settings, or the file contains personal or customer information, contact the IT help desk immediately and mark your message as urgent so the data owner can be informed.

title: Authenticator code rejected even though typed correctly
body: Symptoms: You enter the six-digit code from the authenticator app, but the sign-in page says the code is wrong. You may be asked to try again several times. Cause: The time on your phone may be out of sync, or you may be using a code that has already expired. Sometimes the app shows an account for a different system. Steps: 1. Wait for the code to change and type the new one, entering it quickly. 2. Check that your phone has automatic date and time turned on in its settings. 3. Restart the authenticator app and try again. 4. Confirm the account name in the app matches the work system you are signing in to. 5. If the code still fails, sign out of the sign-in page and start again from the beginning. Still stuck? If the code keeps failing, do not keep guessing, because too many attempts can lock your account. Contact the IT help desk and tell them the time shown on your phone.

title: Video call invitation asks you to share your screen
body: Symptoms: You receive a meeting invitation from someone you do not know, or from a known name in an unexpected message. During the call, they ask you to share your screen or allow remote control of your laptop. Cause: Scammers use video calls to see private information or take control of a device while pretending to be support or a senior colleague. Steps: 1. Do not accept screen sharing or remote control requests from people you cannot verify. 2. End the call and check the sender through a known phone number or the company directory. 3. If you already started sharing, close the sharing window and sign out of any open work apps. 4. Change your work password through the usual company page on a device you trust. 5. Tell the IT help desk the name shown on the invitation and the time of the call. Still stuck? If the caller saw passwords or files, or you allowed control of your laptop, contact the IT help desk immediately so they can check your account and device.

title: Chat message from a colleague asking for gift cards
body: Symptoms: A message arrives in the chat app from a name you recognise, often a manager or senior colleague. It asks you to buy gift cards urgently, scratch the codes, and send them back for a client or staff reward. Cause: The account may have been copied, or a person may be using a fake profile with a similar name. Scammers use urgency to stop you from checking first. Steps: 1. Do not buy any gift cards or send money. 2. Contact the person through another route, such as a phone call or a known email address. 3. Check the sender name and profile picture for small differences in spelling. 4. Report the message to the IT help desk and keep a screenshot. 5. Block the sender in the chat app if you confirm the request was not genuine. Still stuck? If you already bought gift cards or shared the codes, contact your bank or card provider as soon as possible and tell the IT help desk what happened, including the time and the amount spent.

title: QR code on a poster or email leads to a strange page
body: Symptoms: You scan a QR code with your phone and a page opens asking you to sign in, download a file, or confirm your details. The address may look unfamiliar or the page may load oddly. Cause: QR codes can hide web addresses that you cannot read. Criminals can place fake codes on posters, parking meters, or emails to send you to harmful pages. Steps: 1. Do not enter any password or personal details on the page. 2. Close the page and do not download anything it offers. 3. Only scan codes from trusted sources, such as official company notices. 4. If a code is in an email, type the company address into your browser instead of scanning. 5. Report the poster or email to the IT help desk, and take a photo of the code and its location. Still stuck? If you already entered your password, change it right away through the usual company page and tell the IT help desk so they can check your account for unusual sign-ins.

title: Unexpected package or device delivered to your desk
body: Symptoms: A parcel arrives addressed to you or your team, containing a small device, a memory card, or a cable you did not order. There may be a note asking you to plug it in or connect it to your laptop. Cause: Criminals sometimes send devices to staff to test whether they will connect them to company equipment, which can install harmful software or collect information. Steps: 1. Do not connect the device to your laptop, phone, or any company system. 2. Keep the packaging and the note, and avoid touching the device more than needed. 3. Move the parcel to a safe, locked area away from busy desks. 4. Tell your manager and the IT help desk what arrived, including the delivery date and sender details. 5. Follow the security team instructions for collection or disposal. Still stuck? If you already connected the device, unplug it immediately, switch off your laptop, and contact the IT help desk right away so they can check your equipment before you use it again.

title: Password reset email you did not request
body: Symptoms: You receive an email saying a password reset was requested for your work account, but you did not ask for one. The email may include a button to reset now or a warning that your account will be locked within 24 hours. Cause: Someone may be trying to take over your account, or a stranger entered your email address into a reset form by mistake. Attackers often send these alerts to push you into clicking a fake link. Steps: 1) Do not click any button or link in the email. 2) Type the company portal address yourself into your browser, sign in, and open the security page in your account settings. 3) Check whether a reset request is listed there. 4) If nothing unusual appears, delete the email and tell IT in the chat app. 5) If you already clicked a link or entered a code, change your password right away through the portal, not through the email. 6) Forward the original email to the security mailbox as an attachment. Still stuck? Call the IT help desk from a known number and say you received an unexpected password reset email.

title: Real portal shows a certificate warning
body: Symptoms: You open the company portal from your normal bookmark, but your browser shows a red warning saying the site certificate is invalid or the connection is not private. The page may still load if you click past the warning. Cause: Either the portal certificate has expired or been changed during maintenance, or the connection is being intercepted by a fake site or a faulty network device. Clicking past warnings is risky because it can expose your password. Steps: 1) Do not click past the warning or enter your password. 2) Close the browser tab and try again after five minutes. 3) Check whether colleagues can open the portal and whether IT has posted a maintenance notice in the chat app. 4) Try the portal on your phone using mobile data instead of office Wi-Fi. 5) If the warning only appears on office Wi-Fi, disconnect and report the network name to IT. 6) Take a screenshot of the warning, including the web address shown. Still stuck? Contact the IT help desk and send the screenshot so they can check whether the certificate or network is at fault.

title: Authenticator app codes stopped working after a phone upgrade
body: Symptoms: After you upgraded or replaced your phone, the authenticator app shows no codes or asks you to set up your account again. Sign-in codes you used before no longer work, and you may be locked out of the company portal. Cause: Authenticator codes are tied to the phone they were set up on. Moving to a new phone without transferring the account, or restoring a backup that does not include the authenticator data, breaks the link. Steps: 1) Do not guess codes, because repeated wrong attempts can lock your account. 2) Check whether your old phone is still available and still has the authenticator app open. 3) If it is, use the transfer or export option in the authenticator app to move the account to your new phone. 4) If the old phone is gone, ask IT to reset your authenticator enrolment. 5) Confirm your identity in person or by the approved callback method before IT resets anything. 6) Once back in, set up the authenticator again and test one sign-in. Still stuck? Call the IT help desk from your desk phone and ask for an authenticator reset.

title: Voicemail asking you to call an unknown number back
body: Symptoms: You receive a voicemail or missed call notice saying there is an urgent problem with your account, a payment, or a delivery, and asking you to call a number you do not recognise right away. The message may sound automated or rushed and may mention a deadline. Cause: This is a common phone scam designed to make you call a number controlled by a criminal, who will then ask for passwords, codes, or payment details. Steps: 1) Do not call the number back. 2) Write down the number, the time, and what the message said. 3) Look up the official contact number for the department named in the message on the company directory, not on the voicemail. 4) Call that official number to check whether anything is really wrong. 5) Never read out a verification code or password to anyone who calls you. 6) Report the voicemail to the security mailbox with the details you wrote down. Still stuck? Contact the IT help desk and describe the voicemail so the security team can warn colleagues.
